I'll produce a comprehensive evidence paper on AMLO's Mexico in 2022 for Chapter 5B, drawing on the OECD Economic Survey Mexico 2022.

# Evidence Paper: AMLO, Mexico, 2022 — Chapter 5B (Economic Stewardship)

**Source:** OECD Economic Surveys: Mexico 2022 (Volume 2022/4), published February 2022. Reviewed by the Economic and Development Review Committee 22 November 2021; final approval 10 December 2021. Authors: Alberto González Pandiella, Alessandro Maravalle (under Aida Caldera Sánchez). The Survey covers the period through late 2021 and projections through 2023–2024.

**Source role note:** The OECD is an international organization. Its recommendations are advisory; implementation depends on the Mexican government. The Survey is descriptive of, and prescriptive about, AMLO administration policy choices.

---

## 1. The Setting Inherited at the Start of 2022

### 1.1 Macroeconomic Framework and Pandemic Shock

The Survey frames Mexico as having possessed a "solid macroeconomic policy framework, underpinned by an innovative debt management, sound monetary policy and a flexible exchange rate" that "safeguarded macroeconomic stability" during the pandemic (p. 14, UNIT 16). The COVID-19 recession was deep: GDP contracted 8.2% in 2020, with private consumption falling 10.5% and gross fixed capital formation falling 17.8% (Table 1, p. 9, UNIT 11). Manufacturing exports were above pre-pandemic levels by early recovery, while services lagged. The last COVID wave peaked January 2022, with 64% of the population having received at least one vaccine dose and 60% fully vaccinated as of 30 January 2022 (p. 17, UNIT 19).

### 1.2 Pre-Existing Structural Weaknesses

Growth had been "low over the past two decades" (p. 14, UNIT 16), and the potential growth rate had fallen from about 3% in 2015 to 1.6% projected for 2023, "due to a falling contribution of productivity to growth and, following weakness in investment, to a negative contribution of capital" (p. 41, UNIT 43). Informality stood at around 55% of workers (Figure 1.27, p. 45, UNIT 47). Educational inequalities were large: PISA 2018 showed the gap between top and bottom students equivalent to four years of schooling (p. 61, UNIT 64). The 5-year average real GDP growth was -0.4% versus OECD +0.8% (Basic Statistics, p. 7, UNIT 9).

### 1.3 Pre-Existing Fiscal Stance

Mexico had "the lowest tax-to-GDP ratio in the OECD" (Figure 1.14, p. 29, UNIT 31). Tax revenues were 13.1% of GDP in 2019 and 14.3% in 2020. Public spending was 30.1% of GDP (OECD 48.5%) and public debt was 61.0% gross / 52.4% net (OECD 108.9% / 68.1%) (Basic Statistics, p. 7, UNIT 9). The Survey acknowledges Mexico had been "fiscally prudent over the years, broadly meeting its fiscal targets and ensuring fiscal sustainability" but "largely achieved by cutting spending, particularly public investment" (p. 27, UNIT 29).

---

## 2. Fiscal and Tax Policy

### 2.1 Pandemic Response Magnitude

The Survey characterises Mexico's initial fiscal response as "one of the lowest among emerging markets." Public spending increased by around 0.7% of GDP during COVID-19, compared to 4.4% of GDP in emerging economies (p. 23, UNIT 25). The government "opted for reallocating spending from operative spending towards social and health, increasing public sector programmable spending on social protection and health by 0.7 and 0.4 percentage points respectively in 2020, relative to 2019" (p. 23, UNIT 25).

Box 1.1 (p. 18, UNIT 20) lists the specific measures:
- Health expenditure increased by 0.4% of GDP in 2020.
- Frontloaded payments of old-age non-contributory pensions by 8 months.
- Accelerated procurement processes and VAT refunds.
- Loans to SMEs maintaining payrolls (Créditos a la Palabra para empresas), and to domestic/independent workers (Créditos a la Palabra para personas).
- Liquidity support and guarantees by development banks.
- 3-month mortgage subsidy for unemployed workers with Infonavit mortgages.
- Central Bank cut rates 300–325 basis points from March 2020 through February 2021; central bank liquidity facilities amounting to 3.5% of GDP.
- Temporary accounting changes allowing 6-month loan deferrals.
- Reduction of monetary regulation deposits for commercial banks.

### 2.2 Fiscal Aggregates and Path

Public balance was -2.9% of GDP in 2020 and -2.9% in 2021, projected at -3.2% in 2022 and -3.0% in 2023 (Table 1.4, p. 26, UNIT 28). Net public debt rose from 45.1% of GDP in 2019 to 51.5% in 2020, then 49.9% in 2021, projected stable around 50% in 2022–2023. Gross debt rose from 51.0% to 57.9% before declining to 55.5% in 2021. The fiscal stance "while remaining cautious, is less restrictive than foreseen in the 2021 budget. This is a welcome change, as it will mildly support the ongoing recovery" (p. 24, UNIT 26).

"The ability of Mexico's fiscal policy to smooth cycles and support growth during recessions is hampered by a lower tax base than in peer countries, together with a country-risk premium and foreign exchange rate, which increases the cost of servicing debt, and weak automatic stabilisers on the spending side (e.g. there is no unemployment benefits system in place at the Federal level)" (p. 28, UNIT 30).

### 2.3 Tax Administration Measures

Box 1.2 (pp. 25–26, UNIT 27) reports measures implemented in 2019–2020:
- **Elimination of universal compensation (2019):** VAT positive balances could no longer be offset against other taxes automatically. "Increased tax revenues by 0.5% of GDP in 2020."
- **Strengthening sanctions (2020):** Tax fraud classified as serious criminal offence; fake invoices classified as organised crime.
- **BEPS implementation (2020):** 5 of 15 BEPS Actions implemented. "Could increase revenues by up to 0.4 percentage points of GDP by 2024."
- **Taxing digital services (2020):** VAT applied to international intermediation platforms; income tax withholding on certain platform transactions.
- **Phasing out tax expenditures:** Change in fuel pricing methodology increased tax revenues; SME toll-road and mining/rail diesel tax expenditures reduced.
- **General anti-avoidance rule:** Tax authorities may re-characterise transactions lacking business purpose.

Table 1.5 (p. 28, UNIT 30) tracks past OECD recommendations: Mexico "broadly met" its fiscal targets, implemented several tax administration measures, but took **no action** on:
- Increasing progressivity of personal income tax (lowering the top-rate threshold)
- Establishing an independent fiscal council
- Revising the Ley de Coordinación Fiscal

### 2.4 Tax Expenditures and Base

Tax expenditures totalled about 3% of GDP in 2020. VAT tax expenditures: 1.4% of GDP (zero-rating 1.2%, exemptions 0.3%). Corporate income tax expenditures: 0.5% of GDP. Personal income tax expenditures: 0.9% of GDP (Table 1.6, p. 33, UNIT 35). The Survey notes: "Personal income tax expenditures are also large and regressive. Multiple tax allowances and exemptions narrow significantly the tax base… Some of these deductions are generous, in particular, when combined together, and tend to benefit most affluent taxpayers… Inefficient or regressive expenditures amount to at least 0.7% of GDP (IMF, 2020)" (p. 33, UNIT 35).

The income threshold for the top PIT rate is "very high in international perspective" (Figure 1.18, Panel C, p. 32, UNIT 34). The VAT revenue ratio is low (Figure 1.19, p. 33, UNIT 35).

### 2.5 Subnational Taxes

States collect vehicle tax; municipalities collect property tax (predial). "Less than half of states raise vehicle taxes" (p. 34, UNIT 36). Mexico "lacks a comprehensive nation-wide property register" (p. 34, UNIT 36). Table 1.5 reports a cadastral information platform is being created and legal adjustments are discussed in the Senate. Federal transfers amount to 92% of total subnational resources, "the largest share among OECD countries with decentralised government structures" (Box 1.3, p. 35, UNIT 37).

### 2.6 Régimen de Confianza

"Recently announced a new tax scheme (Régimen de confianza in Spanish), targeted at self-employed and SMEs. The scheme includes flat tax rates based on revenues, reduces accounting requirements and facilitates computations by using pre-loaded information. This seem a promising initiative, with a large number of potential beneficiaries (21 million of self-employed and 2 million SMEs)" (p. 34, UNIT 36).

### 2.7 Fiscal Rules Framework

Box 1.4 (p. 35, UNIT 37) describes three fiscal rules:
1. **Balanced budget rule:** Federal budget may run deficit up to 2% of GDP only if due to public investment by federal government and certain SOEs (such as Pemex).
2. **Public sector borrowing requirement (PBSR) rule:** Target specified in budget; requires non-increasing net public debt path.
3. **Structural current spending rule:** Real growth of structural current spending capped at potential output growth. "As a result the rule covers 36% of public sector expenditure."

The Survey judges: "The rules do not provide a truly countercyclical policy framework and tend to favour pro-cyclical fiscal stances. The two budget balance rules favour that fiscal targets are met through discretionary spending cuts and they lack a link with a medium-term fiscal anchor" (p. 35, UNIT 37). It recommends introducing a debt limit, replacing the two balanced budget rules, complemented with an enhanced spending rule. Stabilization funds "do not truly act as countercyclical tools, but mostly as revenue stabilizers" (p. 36, UNIT 38). No fiscal council has been established (Table 1.5).

### 2.8 Public Investment and Infrastructure

The 2022 budget raised capital spending to 3.1% of GDP (from 2.7% in 2019), "the highest level since 2016, although it is foreseen a gradual fall throughout 2023 and 2024" (p. 27, UNIT 29). Social protection spending rose to 5.1% of GDP in 2022 (from 3.8% in 2018). The "increase in public investment needed to close the infrastructure gap in Mexico was estimated to be 1.3 percentage points of GDP a year (Woetzel et al., 2017)" (p. 27, UNIT 29). The Survey recommends that "Conducting rigorous and transparent cost-benefit analysis would ensure sound project selection."

A "partnership established between the federal government and the private sector to launch a pipeline of infrastructure projects is a valuable initiative… The pipeline covers 67 projects, financed by the private sector, and amounting to 2.1% of GDP (Hacienda, 2021)" (p. 47, UNIT 49).

### 2.9 Debt Management

Mexican debt management is described as "sound and innovative" (p. 36, UNIT 38). "Having 60% of debt at fixed rates also mitigates the impact of higher interest rates" (p. 36, UNIT 38). In September 2020 Mexico became the first country to issue a sustainable sovereign bond linked to the UN SDGs (EUR 750 million, 7-year, 1.35% coupon), followed by a 15-year bond in 2021 (Box 1.6, p. 37, UNIT 39). The framework "intends to identify and select those budgetary items targeting states and municipalities with the highest social gap index… 899 municipalities (equivalent to 13 million of inhabitants out of national population of about 130 million) were selected."

### 2.10 PEMEX Support

"Market participants continue to assess PEMEX (the state oil and gas company) as a significant contingent liability for the sovereign (Moody's, 2021)… Current support amounts to about 1% of GDP. PEMEX is the most indebted oil company in the world and the ninth most indebted company in the world considering all sectors. Its debt currently stands at about 10% of Mexican GDP. Contingent pension liabilities are also large, amounting to 6.7% of GDP (Hacienda, 2021)" (p. 38, UNIT 40).

"The authorities aim at strengthening energy security and build an energy system more resilient against natural disasters. With that aim, the role of PEMEX is being enlarged by boosting production and increasing refining activities, including by building new refineries. Such strategy may generate higher refining operating losses in the short and medium term, triggering additional risks for the sovereign" (p. 38, UNIT 40).

"PEMEX production increased during 2020 after a fall that averaged 4% during the previous 14 years" (p. 38, UNIT 40). The Survey recommends aligning PEMEX governance with OECD SOE Guidelines (2015).

---

## 3. Monetary Policy

### 3.1 Banxico Actions

"The Central Bank cut the target interest rate 325 basis points" since the outbreak of the crisis (p. 38, UNIT 40). The Central Bank also "put in place significant liquidity and credit facilities amounting to 3.5% of GDP, a forbearance scheme and a swap line with both the United States Federal Reserve and the United States Treasury to support dollar funding" (p. 38, UNIT 40).

### 3.2 Inflation Response

Headline inflation reached 5.7% in 2021, projected at 5.4% in 2022 and 3.4% in 2023 (Table 1, p. 9, UNIT 11). "The central bank increased rates in its last six meetings, leaving the rate at 6%, as it perceived that shocks weighing on inflation, while transitory, could affect price formation processes and long-term inflation expectations" (p. 39, UNIT 41). The Survey recommends "Gradually increase the interest rate if inflation does not return to the 3% target. Tighten at a faster pace if long-term inflation expectations start to rise" (p. 12, UNIT 14).

Box 1.7 (p. 40, UNIT 42) shows heterogeneous pass-through: 0.97 for reference firm lending rate, 0.43 for mortgage (adjusts in ~1 year), 0.80 for consumer credit (2 months), 0.36 for automotive loans (3 months).

### 3.3 Central Bank Independence

"Since the central bank's autonomy came into effect in the mid-1990s, inflation and its volatility have significantly reduced (Figure 1.22), thanks to the robust inflation targeting framework and flexible exchange rate regime" (p. 40, UNIT 42). The multi-year inflation target is 3% (defined 2003). The Survey states: "Preserving legal and constitutional central bank autonomy and maintaining price stability as its principal mandate is fundamental" (p. 40, UNIT 42).

---

## 4. Investment, Productivity, and Competition

### 4.1 Investment Trends

"Investment has been muted since 2015 (Figure 1.29). It did not grow between 2016 and 2018, hampered by uncertainty at that time about the future of trade agreements in North America. It started to fall in 2019, after some existing investment projects were cancelled and global trade tensions" (p. 46, UNIT 48). "Uncertainty about domestic policy settings has remained high, following the renegotiation of established contracts, particularly in the energy sector, where the government pursues a policy of increasing energy security, strengthening the scope of the state owned PEMEX and the electricity public company, and overturning the 2014 reform that promoted private investment" (p. 46, UNIT 48).

"Uncertainty increased at the beginning of 2021 (Figure 1.30), following the approval of the electricity reform bill, perceived as retroactively changing the rules under which investments were made and increasing legal and regulatory uncertainty (IMCO, 2021), whose implementation was suspended by the court" (p. 46, UNIT 48).

### 4.2 Electricity Market Reform

Box 1.11 (p. 64, UNIT 66) details the constitutional reform proposal announced September 2021:
- "Establishes a guaranteed market share of at least 54% for CFE."
- "The constitutional reform also expands CFE's role in the oversight of the sector and eliminates independent sector regulators."
- "CFE would also be in charge of setting tariffs and granting permits."
- "The electricity reform also changes the rules for generators to access the grid, prioritizing the dispatch of electricity generated by the state-owned company."
- "Prior to the reform, access to the grid was based on marginal power generation costs, giving priority to the least expensive generated electricity, which is renewables-based and largely generated by the private sector."

The Executive Summary (p. 11, UNIT 13) reports: "The electricity market reform under discussion proposes to establish a low guaranteed market share of at least 54% for the public electricity company and to eliminate regulatory bodies overseeing competition and granting permits."

The reform is mentioned as a risk: "Ongoing discussions about reform with some potential reversals in the energy sector creates uncertainty, which could further weaken the recovery" (p. 19, UNIT 21).

### 4.3 Oil Market Reform

"A reform of the oil market has also been approved, allowing the Ministry of Energy to suspend the licences already granted to private companies in case of imminent danger to national security, energy security, and the national economy. The Government would be in charge of the operations intervened during the suspension. The reform also adds new conditions, such as a minimum storage capacity, for a company to obtain and keep its permits" (p. 65, UNIT 67).

### 4.4 Renewable Energy Investment

"These reform attempts follows the suspension of long-term auctions for renewable energy generation in 2019. The auctions had triggered a significant flow of foreign direct investment and led to record the lowest price for a large-scale solar in the world (OECD, 2019), also below prices of conventional sources" (p. 64, UNIT 66).

"Mexico is also increasing investment in fossil fuel exploration and extraction and building a new refinery" (p. 11, UNIT 13).

### 4.5 Competition Policy

"Mexico's autonomous competition authority, created in 2013, has been gradually exercising its authority more vigorously. The number of investigations had been increasing until recently. Attracting and retaining skilled staff has been a significant challenge, which has been exacerbated by a budget cut in 2019 and the establishment of salary ceilings for all public entities from the executive branch of government. The application of the salary ceilings was suspended for existing employees but applies to new recruitments and for internal promotions. This implies significant wage cuts for internally promoted staff and lower attractiveness for external candidates, including for positions in the competition authority board, putting at risk the ability of the competition authority to attract skilled staff. The status of the competition authority as an autonomous and independent body has also been challenged, and plans to change legislation to remove that condition and make it dependant on the government were announced, although not pursued" (p. 44, UNIT 46).

"High market power leads to higher prices, with a welfare loss for the poorest 10% Mexicans estimated to reach 31% of their income, compared with 6% for the richest 10% (COFECE, 2018)" (p. 42, UNIT 44).

### 4.6 Informality and Business Regulation

"Improving business regulations at state and municipal, which in some instances remain costly and complex, should be a key building block of that strategy" (p. 10, UNIT 12). "There is also room to improve business regulations, as in some instances they remain costly and complex, hampering the formalization of firms and jobs" (p. 45, UNIT 47).

A reform to reduce outsourcing fraud was "approved in April 2021, and agreed with the private sector after its reformulation. Before the reform, around 20% of formal workers were subcontracted and under an outsourcing scheme. After the reform, subcontracting is only allowed for specialized services that are not part of the main activity of the firm… Around 2.7 million workers have migrated to standard contracts so far and the salary has increased around 12% on average" (p. 58, UNIT 60).

### 4.7 Trade Integration

Exports to the United States represent more than 80% of total exports (Figure 1.31, p. 49, UNIT 51). Services exports "share of services exports is low and smaller than in regional peers" (Figure 1.32, p. 49, UNIT 51). Restrictiveness on services trade is "higher than in most OECD countries" (Figure 1.33, p. 50, UNIT 52). The updated North America trade agreement (USMCA/T-MEC) "can give fresh impetus to growth, as it brings long-term certainty to trade, foreign investment and conflict resolution in the region" (p. 14, UNIT 16).

---

## 5. Anti-Corruption and Governance

### 5.1 Perception and Institutional Framework

"Mexico has been significantly reinforcing its anticorruption framework overtime. Corruption perceptions have slightly fallen over the last years but the gap with OECD and regional peers remains notable (Figure 1.34)" (p. 51, UNIT 53). "The institutional framework to fight corruption has been strengthened but there are implementation gaps. Further progress has been made towards building the National Anticorruption system, with 17 states having so far adapted their subnational policies to the national system and five more expected to do so in the short-term" (p. 51, UNIT 53).

### 5.2 Specific Gaps

"The Head of the Special Prosecutor's Office for Corruption-related Offences have been recently appointed but additional measures are necessary to finalise pending reforms (OECD, 2021). This includes appointing the judges of the Federal Court of Administrative Justice" (p. 51, UNIT 53). "There is also room to strengthen foreign anti-bribery enforcement (OECD, 2021). Over the last 20 years, Mexico has not successfully concluded any case of foreign bribery" (p. 52, UNIT 54).

### 5.3 Public Procurement

"Mexico's use of public procurement is the lowest in the OECD (Figure 1.35), and has been recently further hampered by an increasing use of direct awards and limits to access information" (p. 52, UNIT 54). The Survey recommends: "Strengthen transparency and use of digital tools in public procurement process, and limit direct contracting" (p. 68, UNIT 70).

### 5.4 Platform Statements on Anti-Corruption

Survey recommendations include: "Continue to strengthen the fight against corruption, including by boosting technical expertise in anticorruption agencies" and "Enact legislation to protect those who report suspicions of foreign bribery" (p. 68, UNIT 70).

---

## 6. Social Policy and Distribution

### 6.1 Poverty and Programme Coverage

"The poverty rate, in its multidimensional definition, increased to 44% in 2020, from 42% in 2018 (Coneval, 2021)" (p. 52, UNIT 54). "Social programmes were estimated to prevent 4.6 million people from falling into extreme poverty and 3.3 more in working poverty during the pandemic (Coneval, 2021)" (p. 53, UNIT 55).

"Non-conditional programs, such as scholarships (Benito Juarez programme) and non-contributory pensions (Pensión para el Bienestar de las Personas Adultas Mayores) have become the backbone of social policies (Table 1.11), replacing Prospera, a conditional cash households transfer programme in place for over 21 years" (p. 53, UNIT 55).

"The share of households in the three lowest income deciles receiving monetary transfers has fallen, while for the rest of deciles, it has increased (Figure 1.36)" (p. 56, UNIT 58). The Survey calls for "strengthening efforts to reach more households in the lowest income deciles by strengthening means testing."

### 6.2 Programme Fragmentation

"The number of programmes run by the federal government has fallen from 272 in 2009 to 123 in 2021. Over half of these programmes (57%) are delivered directly and have a register of beneficiaries, while the rest are delivered through intermediaries… There are also 1444 programs run by states and 6829 run by municipalities (CONEVAL, 2021)" (p. 56, UNIT 58).

### 6.3 Minimum Wage

"Minimum wages, which were lower than in most OECD countries relative to median income (Figure 1.38), have been increased by 50% in real terms from 2019 to 2021. Further increases in the minimum wage are planned until 2024, until the minimum wage allows purchasing two basic consumption baskets (it covers currently 1.3 baskets). Around 13% of full-time workers earn the minimum wage (Conasami, 2021)" (p. 58, UNIT 60). "Previous evaluations suggest that past increases did not harm employment in the lower part of the distribution (Conasami, 2019) but further evaluations of recent increases are warranted" (p. 58, UNIT 60).

### 6.4 Pension Reform

"Starting in 2023, employer's contributions will increase gradually over 8 years, 1% per year, from 5.5% to 13.87%. The number of minimum years to access pensions has been lowered from 25 to 15 years… Government estimates suggest that the reform will expand access, reaching 80% of formal workers once the reform is fully implemented. Replacement rates would increase, particularly for low-income workers… Pension funds' assets will increase from 17% of GDP today to 40% in 2038" (p. 59, UNIT 61).

"The reform of contributory pension system… implies some savings for the budget over the next two decades. Conversely, recent rises in non-contributory pensions will increase spending. Public health expenditures have been estimated to rise by 1.5% of GDP by 2065 (IDB, 2021)" (p. 28, UNIT 30).

"Spending on pensions is expected to increase to 5.3% of GDP in 2026, from the current 4%" (p. 59, UNIT 61). Currently only 30% of the population gets a pension (p. 59, UNIT 61).

### 6.5 Labour Justice Reform

"A new labour justice system, with more emphasis on conciliation… Before the reform, it took four years to resolve a labour dispute… The reform created new independent and specialized courts, the so-called centres for labour conciliation and registration. They are expected to facilitate a quicker and more independent resolution of disputes. The target is that at least 60% of conflicts between workers and companies get resolved through these new conciliation bodies. When a conciliatory agreement is not reached, oral trials should allow a resolution in less than 6 months" (p. 57, UNIT 59).

### 6.6 Insurance and Unemployment

"All OECD countries except Mexico have in place an unemployment benefits system" (p. 53, UNIT 55). "Some states, such as Mexico City, have an insurance scheme, but the full benefits of the tool to pool resources that can be deployed during a downturn can only be achieved if the insurance scheme were established at federal level" (p. 53, UNIT 55).

### 6.7 Health System

"Institute of Health for Well-being (INSABI) was created in January 2020, aiming at offering universal and free health coverage. INSABI, whose start was disrupted by the pandemic, faces significant challenges. The share of the population that reports lacking access to health services increased to 28% in 2020, from 16% in 2018 (Coneval, 2021), even if they are entitled to coverage by INSABI" (p. 59, UNIT 61).

### 6.8 Gender and Care

"Mexican women suffer from a 10% pay gap" (p. 59, UNIT 61). "There has been some progress overtime in extending the coverage of early childhood education and care but there remains a gap with OECD countries or regional peers such as Chile or Colombia. Recently a network of childcare facilities (Estancias Infantiles), that workers could access free of charge, was replaced by subsidies. But the subsidy was insufficient to cover the cost and the number of recipients was reduced" (p. 60, UNIT 62).

"Female labour force participation at 45% is low" (p. 12, UNIT 14). "The share of women in Congress has been on an increasing trend and reaches now 52%. In the current cabinet, 42% of ministers are women, in comparison with 31% in the OECD average (IMCO, 2021). Conversely, Mexico female participation in private company boards, at 7%, is lower than observed in most OECD countries (27% on average)" (p. 61, UNIT 63).

"In Mexico, fathers are entitled to fives day of leave. Contrary to mothers leave that is financed via the Social Security system, fathers leave is fully paid by the employer. Fathers leave take-up has been low" (p. 60, UNIT 62).

### 6.9 Education

"3 millions of Mexicans at primary and secondary education level interrupted their studies and did not restart the 2020-2021 academic year (INEGI, 2021)" (p. 61, UNIT 63). The Survey refers to "one of the longest schools closures in the region and in the OECD" (Figure 1.41, p. 62, UNIT 64).

---

## 7. Climate and Green Policy

### 7.1 Targets and Projections

"Mexico, as in many countries participating in COP26, will be revisiting the 2030 targets during 2022 to align with the Paris agreement temperature goal… In 2015, it committed to reducing greenhouse gas emissions (GHGs) by 22% relative to a business as-usual scenario by 2030, and targets have not been strengthened since then" (p. 63, UNIT 65). "Estimates of environmental harm in Mexico are high, amounting to 4.5% of GDP in 2019" (p. 63, UNIT 65).

### 7.2 Carbon Pricing

"Mexico was a pioneer among emerging economies in taking action on climate change mitigation and adaptation. It was the first emerging economy to introduce carbon price mechanisms" (p. 63, UNIT 65). "The overall carbon price remains low, at about two euro per tonne of emissions (OECD, 2019). This is much lower than the low-end estimate of climate-related cost of carbon emissions of around 60 euros per tonne (Arlinghaus and K. van Dender, 2017)" (p. 63, UNIT 65).

### 7.3 Budget Allocation

"The resources assigned for activities and programs associated with the mitigation and adaptation of climate (Annex 16 in the Federal Budget) increased by 22% in 2021 compared to that assigned for 2020. However, budget allocations for key environmental agencies, such as the Ministry of the Environment and Natural Resources, have decreased overtime (Muller et al., 2021). Programmable spending on environment protection was 0.2% of GDP in 2014 and 0.1% in 2021's budget" (p. 66, UNIT 68).

### 7.4 Climate Finance

"The Ministry of Finance is developing a taxonomy to provide financial players and companies with transparent and consistent definitions of the activities that qualify as sustainable. It is also improving the regulatory framework, by incorporating environmental and social investment policy considerations for institutional investors, such as pension funds, insurance companies and development banks" (p. 22, UNIT 24).

---

## 8. Financial Inclusion and Access to Finance

### 8.1 Banking Sector Indicators

"Only around 47% of the population aged between 18 and 79 years of age held a bank account in Mexico in 2018, less than in other OECD members in the region such as Costa Rica (68%) and Chile (74%)" (p. 77, UNIT 79). "The size of domestic bank credit to the private sector is also low, at around 31.4% of GDP in Mexico in 2021, less than in Brazil (38%), Colombia (45%), Costa Rica (55%) and Chile (100%)" (p. 77, UNIT 79).

### 8.2 SMEs and Credit

"SMEs' access to bank credit is lower than in the average OECD country and regional peers such as Colombia and Chile (Figure 2.5)" (p. 82, UNIT 84). "A high interest rate margin (Figure 2.6, Panel A), well above what is observed in Chile or other OECD countries, is one of the principal barriers to credit for SMEs" (p. 82, UNIT 84).

### 8.3 Competition in Banking

"The three largest banks hold more than 50% of total bank assets (OECD, 2019) and in the banking sector market concentration, which tends to be inversely related to the degree of market competition, has been flat since 2016" (p. 83, UNIT 85). "Concentration is relatively high for consumer loan and mortgages, and low for the business loan market (Figure 2.7). Market concentration is also high in the credit card market" (p. 83, UNIT 85).

### 8.4 Credit Bureaus

"In Mexico there are three companies in charge of collecting credit history information for firms and individuals (credit bureau), two of them belonging to the same economic group. The Competition authority has found anticompetitive practices among these companies. By law these companies are obliged to share the credit history information they compile with the other credit registry companies but the companies belonging to the same group have not done so to protect their monopolistic position (COFECE, 2019)" (p. 84, UNIT 86).

### 8.5 Financial Inclusion Initiatives

Box 2.1 (p. 79, UNIT 81) lists recent initiatives:
- People 15–17 can now open bank accounts; "around 3.5 million bank accounts have been opened" (as of September 2021).
- 10 million bank accounts for beneficiaries of government transfers (mostly 2015–2020).
- 2,700 branches of Banco del Bienestar being constructed; "Banco del Bienestar suspended lending in August 2021 following a sharp rise in the share of non-performing loans."
- Migration banking program.
- "Cobro Digital (CoDi) platform to promote the use of digital payment services. As of October 2021, there are about 10.8 million accounts activated for the use of CoDi."
- 2021 financial reform (July/September 2021) simplified correspondent banking, reduced capital weights for SME/consumer/mortgage credit risk, and adjusted loan reserve calculations for women borrowers.

### 8.6 Capital Markets

"The number of companies listed in the stock market is lower than in some peer countries such as Chile and Peru (Figure 2.9)" (p. 86, UNIT 88). "Only one IPO has taken place in the last three years, as companies have opted for non-traditional structures, including strategic trade sales, rather than Mexico's stock exchange. This contrasts with buoyant recent IPO activity in Brazil, with 26 IPOs registered in 2020 and another 28 only in the first semester of 2021" (p. 86, UNIT 88). "The reduction of IPO exit taxes from 30 percent to 10 percent in 2019 was a positive step to boost IPO activity, but the impact has been so far negligible" (p. 86, UNIT 88).

### 8.7 Fintech Law

"Mexico was a pioneer with the Fintech law in 2018, however, its full effects have not yet materialised since a slow authorisation process of new fintech firms was experienced in part related to a natural learning curve experienced during the initial phase of implementation of the law. However, the aforementioned challenges are expected to dissipate over time. As of mid-October 2021, out of the around 76 fintech firms who demanded for operating in the digital payment and crowdfunding markets, 17 have received full authorisation and 37 a conditional authorisation" (p. 110, UNIT 112).

Technical disruptions and fraud are rising: "Technical disruptions that limit the availability of digital payments are frequent and the number of digital frauds is increasing, with online financial frauds representing 70% of all financial frauds in the first quarter of 2021" (p. 110, UNIT 112).

### 8.8 Digitalisation

"The number of fixed broadband subscriptions per 100 inhabitants is well below the average OECD country" (p. 100, UNIT 102). "Only about 9% of Mexican businesses purchased cloud services against 32% in the average OECD country" (p. 105, UNIT 107). "Only 35% in 2018… accept digital payments" (p. 105, UNIT 107).

## 9. Coverage and Sources of Skepticism

### 9.1 IMF Fiscal Comparison

The Survey's framing of Mexico's fiscal response as low is based on the IMF Database of Country Fiscal Measures: "Public spending increased by around 0.7% of GDP, compared to 4.4% of GDP in emerging economies" (p. 23, UNIT 25). The Survey shows Mexico at the lowest end of the chart in Figure 1.11, with the caveat that "the government opted for reallocating spending."

### 9.2 Anticorruption Track Record

"There is also room to strengthen foreign anti-bribery enforcement (OECD, 2021). Over the last 20 years, Mexico has not successfully concluded any case of foreign bribery" (p. 52, UNIT 54). "Enacting specific legislation to protect public and private sector employees who report suspicions of foreign bribery is a necessary step ahead" (p. 52, UNIT 54).

### 9.3 Information Asymmetries

"In Mexico there are three companies in charge of collecting credit history information for firms and individuals (credit bureau), two of them belonging to the same economic group. The Competition authority has found anticompetitive practices among these companies" (p. 84, UNIT 86). "Only a fifth of Mexican companies find judicial proceedings simple and fast (INEGI, 2016), and the enforcement of civil courts judicial ruling is below most OECD countries ((WJP), 2017-2018)" (p. 96, UNIT 98).

### 9.4 PEMEX as Contingent Liability

"Market participants continue to assess PEMEX (the state oil and gas company) as a significant contingent liability for the sovereign (Moody's, 2021)… current support amounts to about 1% of GDP. PEMEX is the most indebted oil company in the world and the ninth most indebted company in the world considering all sectors. Its debt currently stands at about 10% of Mexican GDP" (p. 38, UNIT 40).

### 9.5 Recommendations Not Implemented

Table 1.5 (p. 28, UNIT 30) lists no-action OECD recommendations:
- Increase progressivity of personal income tax by lowering top-rate threshold.
- Establish a non-partisan, independent, adequately-resourced fiscal council.
- Revise the Ley de Coordinación Fiscal to redefine responsibilities.

Forecast (Table 1.2, p. 20, UNIT 22): GDP growth 2.3% in 2022, 2.6% in 2023. Potential growth projected 1.5% in 2022, 1.6% in 2023 (down from 2.0% in 2019). Output gap -9.6% in 2022, -8.7% in 2023.

"The average real GDP per capita of the top three non-oil regions (Ciudad de Mexico, Nuevo León and Baja California Sur) is more than four times as high as that of the last three regions (Chiapas, Oaxaca and Guerrero)" (p. 81, UNIT 83).

## 12. Observable vs. Asserted vs. Interpretation

### 12.1 Observable Facts (per Survey data)
- 2020 GDP -8.2%, 2021 +5.3%, projected 2022 +2.3%.
- Tax-to-GDP ratio lowest in OECD.
- Electricity reform proposal: 54% CFE guaranteed market share, elimination of independent regulators.
- Outsourcing reform April 2021; 2.7 million workers migrated to standard contracts; salaries up 12% on average.
- Labour justice reform: 4-year average dispute resolution reduced to <6 months target.
- Minimum wage up 50% real 2019–2021.
- Pension reform: employer contributions 5.5%→13.87% over 8 years starting 2023.

### 12.2 Subject/Government Assertions
- AMLÓ government asserts electricity reform "ensuring energy security, maintaining conventional plants as backups for renewables and at avoiding the oversupply of renewables permits" (Box 1.11).
- Successor Prospera (Benito Juárez/pensions) described as more efficient and broader.
- Outsourcing reform "agreed with the private sector" (p. 58, UNIT 60).

### 12.3 OECD Interpretation
- "The rules do not provide a truly countercyclical policy framework and tend to favour pro-cyclical fiscal stances" (p. 35, UNIT 37).
- "Uncertainty about domestic policy settings has remained high" (p. 46, UNIT 48).
- "Implementation efforts lag" on anti-corruption (p. 12, UNIT 14).
- "Mexico, as many other OECD countries, will not meet its emission targets (Climate Action Tracker, 2021)" (p. 63, UNIT 65).
- "The share of households in the three lowest income deciles receiving monetary transfers has fallen, while for the rest of deciles, it has increased" (p. 56, UNIT 58) — OECD interpretation of targeting deterioration.

## 13. Limit Conditions of the Evidence

- The Survey covers policy and outcomes through approximately November 2021; projections through 2023. Any 2022-specific policy actions are not captured.
- The Survey is an external assessment, not a government self-report. Assertions about government intent are reconstructions by OECD based on official statements.
- The Survey was finalised 10 December 2021 and published February 2022, so the cutoff for empirical observations is roughly end-2021.
- "Subsequent evaluations of recent increases [in minimum wage] are warranted" — the Survey acknowledges limits of available evaluation evidence.
- The Survey relies on COFECE, Coneval, Banxico, and SHCP data; methodological caveats are noted in source citations but not deeply reviewed.
- The Survey does not contain primary-source assessment of insider whistleblower accounts or comprehensive audit reports.
